title: Medical Ethics, Law and Professionalism
description: Principles of health-care ethics, consent and capacity, confidentiality, end-of-life issues, professional conduct and medical law in Nigeria.

topics.title: Principles of Health-care Ethics
topics.summary: Autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence and justice; ethical frameworks and dilemmas.

notes.b: Beauchamp and Childress's four principles: respect for autonomy (self-determination, informed consent, truth-telling), beneficence (acting in the patient's best interests), non-maleficence ('first, do no harm' — balancing risks and benefits) and justice (fair distribution of resources and equal treatment). Principles may conflict — e.g. a Jehovah's Witness refusing blood (autonomy vs beneficence), or allocating a single ICU bed (justice). Other frameworks: deontology (duties and rules — Kant), consequentialism (outcomes — utilitarianism), virtue ethics (character — Aristotle), and the doctrine of double effect (e.g. giving opioids to relieve pain at the end of life with the foreseen but unintended effect of shortening life).
k: Deontology vs consequentialism vs virtue ethics

notes.b: The Hippocratic Oath is the historic basis of medical ethics; the World Medical Association's Declaration of Geneva is a modern version. In Nigeria, doctors and dentists are bound by the Code of Medical Ethics issued by the Medical and Dental Council of Nigeria (MDCN), which covers duties to patients, colleagues and society, professional misconduct (e.g. advertising, fee-splitting, sexual relationships with patients, practising under the influence, criminal abortion, negligence) and disciplinary procedures through the Medical and Dental Practitioners Investigating Panel and Disciplinary Tribunal. Nurses, pharmacists and other professionals have equivalent codes from their councils.

topics.title: Informed Consent and Capacity
topics.summary: Elements of valid consent, capacity assessment, minors, emergencies and refusal of treatment.

notes.b: Valid consent must be voluntary (free from coercion), given by a person with capacity, and informed — the patient understands the nature and purpose of the procedure, material risks and benefits, alternatives (including no treatment) and consequences. Consent may be implied (holding out an arm for a blood test), verbal or written (for surgery and significant procedures); a signature is evidence, not the consent itself. The doctor performing the procedure (or a suitably trained delegate) should obtain consent. Patients can withdraw consent at any time. Treating without consent may constitute assault/battery; failing to disclose material risks may constitute negligence.
k: Signature is evidence, not consent itself

notes.b: Capacity is decision-specific: the person must be able to understand the information, retain it, weigh it up and communicate a decision; capacity is presumed in adults unless shown otherwise, and an unwise decision does not by itself mean incapacity. For children (under 18 in Nigeria under the Child Rights Act 2003), consent is usually given by a parent or guardian; mature minors' views should be respected and involved (Gillick competence concept). In emergencies, when a patient lacks capacity and no one can consent, doctors may give necessary treatment in the patient's best interests. Adults with capacity (e.g. Jehovah's Witnesses refusing blood) may refuse treatment even if life-saving; courts may be approached in disputes concerning children.

topics.title: Confidentiality, Truth-telling and Records
topics.summary: Duty of confidentiality and its exceptions, breaking bad news, and data protection.

notes.b: Health professionals must keep patient information confidential; trust depends on it. Disclosure is justified with the patient's consent, when required by law (e.g. notifiable diseases, court orders), or in the public interest to prevent serious harm to others (e.g. a patient with uncontrolled epilepsy who continues to drive a commercial vehicle, or a risk of serious violence). HIV status is highly sensitive: the HIV/AIDS (Anti-Discrimination) Act 2014 protects people living with HIV from discrimination; partner notification should be encouraged and supported, with disclosure without consent considered only as a last resort under strict conditions. Discussing patients in public places or social media, or sharing images without consent, breaches confidentiality. The Nigeria Data Protection Act (2023) governs personal data, including health data.
k: No patient details on social media

notes.b: Patients have a right to honest information about their condition, delivered sensitively. Families sometimes ask doctors to withhold a diagnosis (e.g. cancer) — the doctor should explore their concerns but generally not deceive a competent patient who wishes to know. The SPIKES protocol for breaking bad news: Setting (private, seated, time), Perception (what the patient knows), Invitation (how much they want to know), Knowledge (give information clearly in small chunks, avoid jargon, warning shot), Emotions (respond with empathy), Strategy and Summary (plan and follow-up). Clinical records must be accurate, contemporaneous and secure; patients generally have a right to access their records.

topics.title: End-of-Life Care and Difficult Decisions
topics.summary: Palliative care, withholding and withdrawing treatment, DNACPR, euthanasia, brain death and organ donation.

notes.b: Palliative care improves quality of life for patients with life-threatening illness and their families through pain and symptom relief, psychosocial and spiritual support, from diagnosis onwards. Withholding or withdrawing futile treatment is ethically equivalent and acceptable when treatment no longer benefits the patient, after discussion with the patient (if possible) and family. Do-not-attempt-cardiopulmonary-resuscitation (DNACPR) decisions should be made in advance, documented and communicated. Euthanasia (intentionally ending a patient's life) and physician-assisted suicide are illegal in Nigeria and contrary to the MDCN code; providing adequate analgesia is not euthanasia (double effect).

Brain death (death by neurological criteria) is the irreversible loss of all brain function including the brainstem, diagnosed by strict clinical criteria (deep coma of known cause, absent brainstem reflexes, apnoea test) after excluding reversible causes (drugs, hypothermia, metabolic disturbance). Organ donation requires consent and must never involve payment or coercion; organ trafficking is illegal and condemned by the Declaration of Istanbul. The National Health Act (2014) regulates organ transplantation in Nigeria, prohibiting the sale of organs. The cadaveric and living donor programmes (e.g. kidney transplantation in several Nigerian centres) must follow ethical guidelines.
k: Brain death: coma, absent brainstem reflexes, apnoea

topics.title: Medical Law, Negligence and Professional Practice
topics.summary: Negligence, medical records as evidence, certification, dual loyalty, and professional development.

notes.b: Medical negligence requires: (1) a duty of care owed to the patient; (2) breach of that duty — failing to meet the standard of a reasonably competent practitioner (Bolam test, modified by Bolitho — the practice must also be logically defensible); (3) damage; and (4) causation (the breach caused the harm). Common causes of claims: diagnostic errors, surgical mistakes (wrong site), medication errors, inadequate consent and poor communication. Good records, informed consent, following guidelines, and open disclosure of errors ('duty of candour') reduce harm and litigation. Criminal liability arises in gross negligence causing death.

Doctors certify births, deaths (medical certificate of cause of death — never falsify), fitness and sickness; issuing false certificates is misconduct. Dual loyalty conflicts arise when obligations to third parties (employers, police, prisons, insurers) conflict with patients' interests — the patient's welfare remains primary, and doctors must never participate in torture. Health workers should avoid conflicts of interest (e.g. accepting inducements from pharmaceutical companies), practise within their competence, pursue continuing professional development (MDCN requires CPD for licence renewal), maintain professional boundaries, and look after their own health (burnout is common; seek help for impairment). Brain drain ('japa') of Nigerian health workers is a major workforce challenge.
k: Patient welfare first in dual loyalty

q: Which is NOT required to prove medical negligence?
